[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Raja_Ravi_Varma.jpg/250px-Raja_Ravi_Varma.jpg?utm_source=en.wikiquote.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/File:Raja_Ravi_Varma.jpg)

Raja Ravi Varma

**[Raja Ravi Varma](link_10)** ([29 April](link_11)[1848](link_12) – [2 October](link_13)[1906](link_14)) from the princely state of [Travancore](link_15) (presently in [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "w:Kerala")). He was widely acclaimed following his winning an award for an exhibition of his paintings at Vienna in 1873. Though his style of painting was described as too showy and sentimental, his paintings are widely popular in India. A large number of his lovely paintings are in the Laxmi Vilas Palace of Vadodara. He has been hailed as one of the “greatest painters in the history of Indian art. His paintings achieved recognition for his depiction of scenes from the epics of the [Mahabharata](link_16) and [Ramayana](link_17).

## Quotes

[[edit](https://en.wikiquote.org/w/index.php?title=Raja_Ravi_Varma&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Quotes")]

*   Who knows if these very pictures, now painted for maharajas, will not find their way to the museums one day. 
    *   Quoted in [Quotations by 60 Greatest Indians](link_18).Dhirubhai Ambani Institute of Information and Communication Technology.Retrieved on 27 November 2013.

*   ...the importance of recovering the customs and the institutions of the past thus inaugurating the archaeological approach to art 
    *   Varma spoke on the occasion of the exhibition of his painting of the Sabine Woman who were supposed to have inspired him .Mitter, Partha(1994)._[Art and Nationalism in Colonial India, 1850-1922: Occidental Orientations](link_19)_. Cambridge University Press. [ISBN 978-0-521-44354-8](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-0-521-44354-8 "Special:BookSources/978-0-521-44354-8").

## Quotes about Varma

[[edit](https://en.wikiquote.org/w/index.php?title=Raja_Ravi_Varma&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Quotes about Varma")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Ravi_Varma-Princess_Damayanthi_talking_with_Royal_Swan_about_Nala.jpg/250px-Ravi_Varma-Princess_Damayanthi_talking_with_Royal_Swan_about_Nala.jpg?utm_source=en.wikiquote.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/File:Ravi_Varma-Princess_Damayanthi_talking_with_Royal_Swan_about_Nala.jpg)

Hamsa Damyanti Painting by Raja Ravi Varma.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Sri_Shivaji_Maharraj.jpg/250px-Sri_Shivaji_Maharraj.jpg?utm_source=en.wikiquote.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/File:Sri_Shivaji_Maharraj.jpg)

Shivaji

*   She quoted HamsDamyanti. According to her it is this painting that Ravi Varma reached the pinnacle of his art in depicting [[w:Maharashtra people}Maharashtrian]] Beauty. Ravi Varma’s talent lay in the mixing of colours and the effect he got when he painted drapery, jewelry and royal clothes. Uma mentions two other paintings of [Rani Lakshmibai](link_20) and princess [Tarabai](link_21)- both of which show Ravi Varma’s remarkable talent in [portraiture](link_22). She also made a special reference to the painting of Krishna and mother displayed in [Mysore Palace](link_23). Uma Varma believes Ravi Varma’s unique talent lay in the fact that no one has yet been able to make an exact replica of hi paintings. She has seen many [European Masters](link_24) copied perfectly but both Uma varma and her daughter Radhika say that they are yet to see painting, which could be an exact copy of Ravi Varma’s paintings. 
    *   Statement by his wife Uma Varma on his best painting talent as told to Ranjit Desai in his novel on Raja Ravi Varma Ranjit Desai._[RAJA RAVI VERMA: A Novel](link_25)_. HarperCollins Publishers India. [ISBN 978-93-5029-662-2](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-93-5029-662-2 "Special:BookSources/978-93-5029-662-2").

*   The more I saw, the more I admired the Master's genius — his uncanny ability, through the magic of his brush to depict mood, emotion and atmosphere and to encapsulate the whole story in the selected scene. I felt even then that a state of the art folio on his works needed to be brought out. Only, I never imagined that it was I who would eventually be doing it. 
    *   Parasram Mangharam, author of _Raja Ravi Varma, The Painter Prince_, in the [_Deccan Herald_ (26 October 2003)](link_26)

*   Ravi Varma is not only among India's greatest artists, but also a great patriot. His depiction of the beauty of the Indian woman is unequalled in Indian art....When the art gallery of Mysore was under renovation, I got an opportunity to photograph them and my joy knew no bounds! Over the years I got to see many a fine-print reproductions of Ravi Varma's paintings and have tried to photograph the expression of his subjects. 
    *   [The Genius of Ravi Verma](link_27).Kamat’s Potpourri.Retrieved on 27 November 2013.

*   He has become an Indian Kilroy. No matter where you look - whether in a book on the history of Indian art or one on advertising and printing in India or even something like popular taste and the making of the Indian national ethos - Raja Ravi Varma is there. 
    *    "[Art of brotherhood](link_28)". Retrieved on 27 November 2013.</ref>

*   This painting [By Varma] takes the view of the 18th century politics …looking at [it] one immediately thinks of the whole …of the great warrior. So he must be congratulated 
    *   Remark by [Tilak](link_29) on Ravi Varma’s painting of [Shivaji](link_30) at the Shivaji Festivals held in Maharashtra. .Mitter, Partha(1994)._[Art and Nationalism in Colonial India, 1850-1922: Occidental Orientations](link_19)_. Cambridge University Press. [ISBN 978-0-521-44354-8](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-0-521-44354-8 "Special:BookSources/978-0-521-44354-8").

### Sources

[[edit](https://en.wikiquote.org/w/index.php?title=Raja_Ravi_Varma&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Sources")]

[Ravi Varma](link_31).Encyclopaedia Britannica.Retrieved on 26 November 2013.

*   Varma was the first Indian to use Western techniques of perspective and composition and to adapt them to Indian subjects, styles, and themes. He won the Governor’s Gold Medal in 1873 for the painting Nair Lady Adorning Her Hair. He became a much-sought-after artist among both the Indian nobility and the Europeans in India, who commissioned him to paint their portraits.
*   His depictions of Indian women drew such appreciation that a beautiful woman would often be described as looking “as if she had stepped out of a Varma canvas.”
*   Varma adapted Western realism to pioneer a new movement in Indian art. In 1894 he set up a lithographic press in order to mass-produce copies of his paintings as oleographs, enabling ordinary people to afford them. That innovation resulted in the tremendous popularity of his images, which became an integral part of popular Indian culture thereafter.

**Kilimanoor** is a panchayat and a town in the [Chirayinkeezhu taluk](link_11) of [Thiruvananthapuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district "Thiruvananthapuram district") in [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"), India.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor#cite_note-2) It is located on [MC/SH 1 Road](link_12), 33 kilometres (21 mi) northwest of the city of Thiruvananthapuram ([Trivandrum](link_13)), 14 km (8.7 mi) east of [Attingal](link_14) and 20 km (12 mi) east of [Varkala](link_15).

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Kilimanoor ("land of the bird and the deer") was ruled by a [Pillai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sai_pillai_meleputhiyakav_(Kerala_title)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sai pillai meleputhiyakav (Kerala title) (page does not exist)") ruling chief and was forfeited to Travancore by Maharaja Marthanda Varma. The estate comprising several villages was then handed over to the family of the father of the King who had come south from Parappanad in Malabar around 1718.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor#cite_note-3) was ruled by a chief during time of the [Ettuveetil Pillamar](link_16) in the kingdom of [Travancore](link_17). The chief rebelled against the [Maharajah](link_18)[Marthanda Varma](link_19), and the region was annexed and later given to the Royal House of Kilimanoor.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAiya1906329-4)

This [Royal House of Kilimanoor](link_20) has a history of more than 300 years. In 1705 (ME 880), the son and two daughters of Ittammar Raja of Beypore Thattarikovilakam, a [Parappanad](link_21) royal house, were adopted by the Royal house of [Venad](link_22). Parappanad was actually the ruling family of [Parappanangadi](link_23) in present-day [Malappuram district](link_24). Ittammar Raja's sister and her sons, Rama Varma and Raghava Varma, settled in Kilimanoor and married the now-adopted sisters. Marthanda Varma, the founder of the [Kingdom of Travancore](link_25) was the son of Raghava Varma. Raghava Varma's nephew, Ravi Varma Koil Thampuran, married Marthanda Varma's sister. Their son came to be known as Dharma Raja Kartika Thirunnal Rama Varma. In 1740, when an allied force led by Dutch Captain Hockert supporting the Deshinganadu king attacked Venad, an army from Kilimanoor tactfully resisted and then defeated them. Although a small victory, this was the first time an Indian army defeated a European power. In recognition of this feat, Marthanda Varma, in 1753, exempted the areas under control of [Kilimanoor Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Palace "Kilimanoor Palace") from taxes and proclaimed autonomous status. The present palace complex was also built during this time along with the Ayyappa temple for the family deity.

Kerala,[a] officially Keralam,[b] is a state on the Malabar Coast of southern India. It was formed on 1 November 1956 under the States Reorganisation Act, which unified the country's Malayalam-speaking regions into a single state. Covering 38,863 km2 (15,005 sq mi), Kerala is primarily a strip of coastal plains sandwiched by the Western Ghats and the Laccadive Sea, bound by Karnataka to the northeast, Tamil Nadu to the east, and the Lakshadweep islands in the western vicinity. With 33 million inhabitants according to the 2011 census, Kerala is the 13th-most populous state in India. Thiruvananthapuram is the capital city while the Kochi metropolitan area is the state's most populated region. Malayalam is the most widely spoken language and, alongside English, serves as an official language of the state.

Kerala has been a prominent exporter of spices since 3000 BCE. The Chera dynasty, the first major kingdom in the region, rose to prominence through maritime commerce but often faced invasions from the neighbouring Chola and Pandya dynasties. In the 15th century, the spice trade attracted Portuguese traders to Kerala, initiating European colonisation in India. After Indian independence in 1947, the kingdoms Travancore and Cochin acceded to the newly formed republic and were merged in 1949 to form the state of Travancore-Cochin. In 1956, the modern state of Kerala was instituted by exchanging peripheral areas with the former Madras State; Malabar district and the Kasargod taluk of South Canara district were merged with Travancore-Cochin to form Kerala, while Kanyakumari district and parts of Shenkottai taluk were annexed to Madras State. Kerala consists of 14 districts since 1984.

Kerala has the highest Human Development Index, at 0.784 in 2018; the highest literacy rate, 96.2% in 2018; the highest life expectancy, at 77.3 years; and the highest sex ratio, with 1,084 women per 1,000 men and the lowest positive population growth rate in India (3.44%). It is the least impoverished and the second-most urbanised state in the country. The state has witnessed significant emigration, particularly to the Arab states of the Persian Gulf during the Gulf Boom of the 1970s and early 1980s, and its economy relies heavily on remittances from a large Malayali expatriate population. Hinduism is practised by more than 54% of the population, followed by Islam and Christianity. The culture is a synthesis of Aryan and Dravidian traditions, shaped over millennia by influences from across India and abroad.

The production of black pepper and natural rubber contributes significantly to the national output. In the agricultural sector, coconut, tea, coffee, cashew, and spices are important crops. The state has a coastline of 595 kilometres (370 mi), and 1.1 million people depend on the fishing industry, which accounts for around 3% of the state's income. The economy is largely service sector oriented, while the primary sector contributes a comparatively smaller share. Kerala has the highest media exposure in India, with newspapers published in nine languages, primarily Malayalam and English. Named as one of the ten paradises of the world by National Geographic Traveler, Kerala is one of the prominent tourist destinations of India, with coconut-lined sandy beaches, backwaters, hill stations, Ayurvedic tourism and tropical greenery as its major attractions. The state has also been repeatedly recognised in international travel rankings for its tourism.

Name
Etymology

The word "Kerala" is first mentioned as Keralaputra[c] ('son of Chera[s]') in a 3rd-century-BCE rock inscription left by the Maurya emperor Ashoka (274–237 BCE) in one of his edicts.[16][17] At that time, one of the three states in the southern part of the Indian subcontinent was known as Cheralam in Classical Tamil. As per linguist Robert Caldwell, Kera and Kela are variants of the word Chera.[17]

There are several theories as to the origin of the word Kerala. Kerala might have originated from the combination of the two words chera and alam meaning 'land of the Cheras'.[15] In Tamil literature, Cheral refers to the oldest known dynasty of the kings who ruled the Kerala region and might have been derived from the Old Tamil word for 'lake'.[18] Keralam may stem from the combination of the words cherive and alam meaning 'land of hill or a mountain slope'.[19] It might also have originated from the Malayalam words kera and alam meaning 'coconut tree' and 'land' respectively, thus meaning 'land of coconuts', due to the abundance of coconut trees in the region.[15][20]

Kerala was also called Malabar, after the eponymous coast. The region was called as malanadu or malavaram meaning 'hill country' due to its topography, which later became 'Malabar'.[15]

Renaming to Keralam

There has been a long-standing demand to change the official English name of the state from Kerala to Keralam, the official name of the state in Malayalam.[21][22] In June 2024, the Kerala Legislative Assembly passed a unanimous resolution to change the state's name from 'Kerala' to 'Keralam', which sought to amend the state's name to reflect its Malayali identity.[23] The proposal was approved by the Union Cabinet on 24 February 2026.[24] After the bill was approved by the Kerala Legislative Assembly on 2 July 2026, the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 was introduced in the Parliament of India.[25] It was approved by the Lok Sabha on 11 August 2026,[26][27][28] and the Rajya Sabha on the next day.[29][30] Following the president's assent, the name change was effected officially on 25 August 2026 after it was notified by the Ministry of Home Affairs of the Government of India.[31]

History
Main article: History of Kerala
Legend
A painting depicting Parashurama, an avatar of Vishnu, commanding Varuna, the Hindu god of ocean, to part the seas

In stories of the Dashavatara from Hindu mythology, the lands of Kerala were recovered from the sea by the axe-wielding warrior sage Parashurama, the sixth avatar (incarnation) of Vishnu. As a result, Kerala is traditionally referred to as Parashurama Kshetram ("The Land of Parashurama").[32] According to legend, Parashurama threw his axe across the sea, and the water receded to the point where it landed. This land that emerged extended from Gokarna to Kanyakumari.[33] The land that emerged was saline and uninhabitable, so Parashurama invoked the snake king Vasuki, who spat holy poison to purify the soil, transforming it into fertile land. Out of respect, Vasuki and all snakes were appointed as guardians of the land. The legend was expanded and codified in the 17th or 18th century text Keralolpathi. It links the origin of early Kerala institutions—such as land tenure and administration—to Parashurama's story.[34] In medieval times, the Chera king Chenkuttuvan may have emulated the Parashurama tradition by throwing his spear into the sea to symbolise his lordship over it.[35]

A prominent Puranic figure associated with Kerala is Mahabali, an asura and archetypal just king who is said to have ruled the earth from Kerala. He defeated the devas in battle, driving them into exile. In response, the devas appealed to Vishnu, who assumed his fifth avatar as Vamana and, to restore order, pushed Mahabali down to Patala (the netherworld). According to popular belief, Mahabali returns to Kerala once a year, which is commemorated as the Onam festival.[36] The Matsya Purana, one of the oldest among the 18 Puranas,[37][38] situates the story of Matsya—the first avatar of Vishnu—and king Manu, the first man and ruler of the region—in the Malaya Mountains of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.[39][40]

Pre-history
A Neolithic dolmen at Marayur

A substantial portion of present-day Kerala is believed to have been submerged under the sea in ancient times. The discovery of marine fossils near Changanassery supports this hypothesis.[41] Prehistoric archaeological discoveries in Kerala include Neolithic-era dolmens in the Marayur region of the Idukki district, locally known as muniyara—from muni (hermit or sage) and ara (dolmen).[42] Rock engravings in the Edakkal caves in Wayanad date back to the Neolithic period, around 6000 BCE.[43][44] Archaeological studies have identified Mesolithic, Neolithic and Megalithic sites throughout the region.[45] These findings indicate that the development of early Kerala society and culture began in the Paleolithic Age and progressed through the Mesolithic, Neolithic and Megalithic periods.[46] Foreign cultural interactions also played a role in shaping this development;[47] some historians suggest possible connections with the Indus Valley Civilisation during the late Bronze Age and early Iron Age.[48]

Ancient history
Spice trade routes (in blue)

Kerala has been a major spice exporter since at least 3000 BCE, according to Sumerian records, and it is continues to be referred to as the "Garden of Spices" or as the "Spice Garden of India".[49][50][51] The region's spices attracted ancient Babylonians, Assyrians, and Egyptians to the Malabar Coast during the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE. Arabs and Phoenicians also established trade links with Kerala during this period.[52] The land of Keralaputra was one of four independent kingdoms in southern India during the time of Emperor Ashoka, alongside the Chola, Pandya, and Satiyaputra kingdoms.[53] Scholars generally identify Keralaputra as another name for the Cheras, the earliest major dynasty based in Kerala.[54][55] Although disputed by some scholars, the mainstream view holds that Malayalam descends from a west coast dialect of Early middle tamil and became a distinct language somewhere between 9 and 13th century. These southern territories once shared a common language and cultural framework, within a region historically known as Tamilakam.[56] While the Cheras governed most of what is now Kerala, the southern tip of the region fell under the control of the Pandyas,[57] whose trading port is sometimes identified in ancient Western sources as Nelcynda (or Neacyndi).[58] Later, control of the region alternated among the Pandyas, Cheras, and Cholas. The Ays and Mushikas were two other dynasties of ancient Kerala, located to the south and north of the Chera territory, respectively.[59][60]

By the last centuries BCE, the coast had become an important hub for Greek and Roman trade, particularly in black pepper. The Cheras maintained commercial links with Ancient China, West Asia, Egypt, Greece, and the Roman Empire. In foreign trade records, the region was referred to as Male or Malabar.[61] Principal ports of the time included Muziris, Berkarai, and Nelcynda.[62] The value of Rome's annual trade with Kerala has been estimated at 50 million sesterces.[63] Contemporary Sangam literature describes Roman ships arriving at Muziris, laden with gold in exchange for pepper. One of the earliest Western traders to navigate the monsoon winds to reach Kerala was Eudoxus of Cyzicus, who made the voyage around 118 or 166 BCE under the patronage of Ptolemy VIII, king of the Hellenistic Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt. Roman establishments in the region's port cities—including a temple of Augustus and barracks for garrisoned Roman soldiers—are recorded in the Tabula Peutingeriana, the only surviving map of the Roman cursus publicus.[64][65]

Merchants from West Asia and Southern Europe established coastal posts and settlements in Kerala.[66] The Jewish connection with Kerala is believed to date back to 573 BCE.[67][68][69] Arab traders had links with Kerala from at least the 4th century BCE; Herodotus (484–413 BCE) noted that goods brought by Arabs from Kerala were sold to Jews in Eden.[62] These Arab traders intermarried with local communities, leading to the formation of the Muslim Mappila community.[70] In the 4th century CE, some Christians migrated from Persia and joined the early Syrian Christian community, which traces its origins to the evangelistic activities of Thomas the Apostle in the 1st century CE.[71][72] The term Mappila—originally an honorific applied to esteemed foreign visitors—later became associated with the descendants of Jewish, Syrian Christian, and Muslim immigrants, leading to the terms Juda Mappilas, Nasrani Mappilas, and Muslim Mappilas, respectively.[73][74] According to the traditions of these communities, some of the earliest religious establishments in India were built in Kerala.[70] These include the Saint Thomas Christian churches,[75] the Cheraman Juma Masjid (established in 629 CE), India's first mosque,[76] and the Paradesi Synagogue (built in 1568 CE), the oldest active synagogue in the Commonwealth of Nations.[77]

Medieval period
Tharisapalli plates granted to Saint Thomas Christians testify that merchant guilds and trade corporations played a very significant role in the economy and social life during the Kulasekhara period.

A second Chera kingdom (c. 800–1102), also known as the Kulasekhara dynasty of Mahodayapuram, was founded by Kulasekhara Varman and governed over a territory comprising most of present-day Kerala and parts of modern Tamil Nadu. During the early phase of the Kulasekara period, the southern region—from Nagerkovil to Thiruvalla—was controlled by the Ay dynasty. By the 10th century, however, the Ays had lost their power, and the region was incorporated into the Kulashekara realm.[78][79] Under Kulashekhara rule, Kerala experienced a flourishing period marked by developments in art, literature, trade, and the Bhakti movement within Hinduism.[80] It was during this time that a distinct Keralite identity began to emerge, separate from Tamil culture, particularly through linguistic differentiation.[81] For administrative purposes, the kingdom was divided into provinces governed by local chieftains called Naduvazhis. Each province was further subdivided into desams, which were overseen by Desavazhis.[80]

A series of Chera–Chola conflicts in the 11th century disrupted foreign trade through Kerala's ports. During this period, Buddhism and Jainism, which had previously coexisted with Hinduism, declined and eventually disappeared from the region.[82] Social structures became increasingly rigid, and caste divisions deepened.[83] The Kulashekhara dynasty ultimately fell in 1102 CE following a combined assault by the Later Pandyas and Later Cholas.[78] In the 14th century, Ravi Varma Kulashekhara (r. 1299–1314) of the southern Venad kingdom briefly established a short-lived supremacy over much of southern India. Following his death, and in the absence of a strong central authority, the region fragmented into thirty small, frequently warring principalities. Among the most powerful were the kingdom of Samuthiri (Zamorin) in the north, Venad in the south and Kochi in the central region. In the 18th century, King Anizham Thirunal Marthanda Varma of Travancore launched a series of military campaigns and annexed territories up to northern Kerala, establishing Travancore as the dominant power in the region. The Kochi ruler sued for peace, and the Malabar region eventually came under direct British rule until Indian independence in 1947.[84][85]

In the early 15th century, the Ming Chinese admiral Zheng He's treasure fleets made repeated stops at the Malabar ports of Kozhikode, Kollam, and Kochi during his seven voyages between 1405 and 1433, establishing formal tributary relations with local rulers including the Zamorin of Calicut.[86][87] Calicut, which Zheng He's interpreter Ma Huan described as a great nation in the Indian Ocean (古里國，即西洋大國也, "The country of Guli, is the great country of the Western ocean"),[88] served as the fleet's principal Indian Ocean trading base, and a stone tablet was erected there around 1409 to commemorate the relationship between China and India, though it no longer survives.[86][89] China also intervened in the rivalry between Calicut and Kochi: for his fifth voyage, Zheng He conferred a seal on the King of Kochi, known to the Chinese as Keyili (可亦里), conferred a Chinese name to a mountain to show Chinese support (named Zhenguo Zhi Shan, 鎮國之山, "Mountain Which Protects the Country"), and delivered a second stone tablet inscribed with a proclamation composed by the Yongle Emperor.[90] Physical and cultural traces of this period persist in Kerala, including the Chinese fishing nets of Kochi, Chinese-derived Malayalam terms for household items such as cheena chatti (wok) and cheena bharani (porcelain jar), and porcelain tiles at the Paradesi Synagogue possibly linked to Chinese gifts.[87][89] Chinese trade with the region declined after Zheng He's death in 1433 traditionally placed at Calicut during the return leg of the seventh voyage, and the subsequent Ming retreat from maritime expansion; the end of the voyages left Kochi exposed to an eventual invasion by the Zamorin of Calicut.[86][87]

Colonial rule
The route taken by Vasco da Gama to reach Kerala (in black)

During the High and Late Middle Ages, Arab traders held a maritime monopoly over the spice trade in the Indian Ocean. This dominance was challenged during the European Age of Discovery when the spice trade—particularly in black pepper—became a major focus of European commercial activity.[91] By the 15th century, the Portuguese had begun asserting control over eastern maritime routes, culminating in Vasco Da Gama's arrival at Kappad, near Kozhikode (Calicut), in 1498.[92][93] The Zamorin of Kozhikode granted the Portuguese permission to trade with his subjects, leading to the establishment of a prosperous Portuguese factory and fort.[94]

**Kilimanoor Palace** is a palace located in [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor "Kilimanoor"), in the Indian state of [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_House_of_Kilimanoor#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_House_of_Kilimanoor#cite_note-2) It is the birthplace of painter [Raja Ravi Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma "Raja Ravi Varma") and Raghava Varma, the father of king [Marthanda Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marthanda_Varma "Marthanda Varma").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_House_of_Kilimanoor#cite_note-Thrippadidaanam-3)

## The Palace

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor_Palace&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: The Palace")]

The Palace complex covers more than six hectares, and comprises the traditional residential structures of Kerala, like the Nalukettu, small and medium-sized buildings, three ponds, wells and sacred groves (_kaavu_).

Raja Ravi Varma is said to have built and maintained some of the buildings from the proceeds of his paintings. Families related to the Travancore royal house continue to live here.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor_Palace&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

The royal house at Choottayil, [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor "Kilimanoor") has a history stretching back more than 300 years, although the oldest buildings are from a much earlier period.

### Association with the Travancore royal house

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor_Palace&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Association with the Travancore royal house")]

In 1705, the son and two daughters of Ittammar Raja of [Beypore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beypore "Beypore") Thattarikovilakam, the northern branch of [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad") royal house, were adopted into the royal house of [Venad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venad "Venad"). The Ittammar Raja's sister and her sons, Rama Varma and Raghava Varma, settled in Kilimanoor and married the now-adopted sisters.

The lands around the present-day palace were a part of an estate which originally belonged to a [Pillai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillai_(Kerala_title) "Pillai (Kerala title)") ruling chief. The estate comprised several villages and was handed over to the family of Raghava Varma.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_House_of_Kilimanoor#cite_note-4)[Maharaja Marthanda Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marthanda_Varma "Marthanda Varma"), the founder of the [Kingdom of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"), was the son of Raghava Varma.

In 1739, after Marthanda Varma ascended the throne, an alliance led by the [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Malabar "Dutch Malabar") Captain Hockert, was formed between [Kochi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Malabar "Dutch Malabar"), [Thekkumkoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thekkumkur "Thekkumkur"), [Desinganadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kollam "Kollam") and [Purakkad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purakkad "Purakkad"), due to their shared enmity towards Marthanda Varma. In 1740, this [allied force attacked Venad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore%E2%80%93Dutch_War#Initial_Dutch_successes "Travancore–Dutch War") and an army from Kilimanoor resisted and subsequently defeated them in the [Battle of Colachel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Colachel "Battle of Colachel"). Although a small victory, this was the first time an Indian army had defeated a European power.

In 1753, in recognition of this feat, Marthanda Varma exempted the areas controlled by the Kilimanoor Palace, as well as most of the area under the present Kilimanoor and [Pazhayakunnummel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazhayakunnummel "Pazhayakunnummel") panchayats from taxes, and granted them autonomous status. **Chirayinkeezhu Taluk** is a [taluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taluk "Taluk") in the district of [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district "Thiruvananthapuram district") in the Indian state of [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu_taluk#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu_taluk#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu_taluk#cite_note-3) It shares a land border with [Varkala Taluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varkala_Taluk "Varkala Taluk") to the North and [Thiruvananthapuram Taluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Taluk "Thiruvananthapuram Taluk") to the South. It comprises 12 panchayats as well as [Attingal Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal"). Chirayinkeezhu taluk is the birthplace of several distinguished personalities, including the renowned painter [Raja Ravi Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma "Raja Ravi Varma"), poet and social reformer [Kumaran Asan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumaran_Asan "Kumaran Asan"), and the actor [Prem Nazir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prem_Nazir "Prem Nazir").

## Settlements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chirayinkeezhu_taluk&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Settlements")]

There are 16 villages and one [municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipality "Municipality") in the taluk.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu_taluk#cite_note-4)

### Villages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chirayinkeezhu_taluk&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Villages")]

[Alamcode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alamcode,_Thiruvananthapuram "Alamcode, Thiruvananthapuram"), [Azhoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azhoor "Azhoor"), [Chirayinkeezhu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu "Chirayinkeezhu"), [Edakkode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edakkode "Edakkode"), [Kadakkavoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kadakkavoor "Kadakkavoor"), [Keezhattingal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keezhattingal_(Village) "Keezhattingal (Village)"), [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor "Kilimanoor"), [Ponganadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponganadu "Ponganadu"), [Koonthalloor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koonthalloor "Koonthalloor"), [Koduvazhannoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koduvazhannoor "Koduvazhannoor"), [Mudakkal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudakkal "Mudakkal"), [Nagaroor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagaroor "Nagaroor"), [Pazhayakunnummel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazhayakunnummel "Pazhayakunnummel"), [Perunguzhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perunguzhi "Perunguzhi"), [Pulimath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulimath "Pulimath"), [Sarkara-Chirayinkeezhu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarkara-Chirayinkeezhu "Sarkara-Chirayinkeezhu"), [Vakkom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vakkom "Vakkom"), [Vellalloor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vellalloor "Vellalloor")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu_taluk#cite_note-5)

### Municipalities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chirayinkeezhu_taluk&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Municipalities")]

Municipality of [Attingal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal") is the only one in the taluk

## Places of tourist interest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chirayinkeezhu_taluk&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Places of tourist interest")]

Chirayinkeezh has a network of [backwaters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_backwaters "Kerala backwaters") and [canals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canals "Canals"), which is quite typical of [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"). Also there are many [Temples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temples "Temples") and important tourist places. Some of them are given below.

**[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia "w:Wikipedia")** is a free content, multilingual online encyclopedia written and maintained by a community of volunteers through a model of open collaboration, using a wiki-based editing system. Individual contributors, also called editors, are known as Wikipedians. Wikipedia is the largest and most-read reference work in history.

## Quotes

[[edit](https://en.wikiquote.org/w/index.php?title=Wikipedia&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Quotes")]

### 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikiquote.org/w/index.php?title=Wikipedia&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 2000s")]

#### 2000

[[edit](https://en.wikiquote.org/w/index.php?title=Wikipedia&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2000")]

*   **What if we could get everyone in the world together to record what they know in one place?**
    *   [Jimmy Wales](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Jimmy_Wales "Jimmy Wales"), when recruiting [Larry Sanger](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Larry_Sanger "Larry Sanger") in January 2000,[The early history of Wikipedia (part 1)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2c9mRKFy5fU) (1:49), Larry Sanger (7 May 2010)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Wikipedia_app_iOS.jpg/250px-Wikipedia_app_iOS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikiquote.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/File:Wikipedia_app_iOS.jpg)

A view of the [Wikipedia App](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia%20App "wikipedia:Wikipedia App"), the official [app](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Application%20software "wikipedia:Application software") of Wikipedia. Any user can install Wikipedia, and you can install, before this, the Wikipedia App to download Wikipedia free and for this, a user need to go to 
[https://github.com/wikimedia/wikipedia-ios](https://github.com/wikimedia/wikipedia-ios)
 or to [https://github.com/wikimedia/apps-win8-wikipedia](https://github.com/wikimedia/apps-win8-wikipedia)

#### 2001

[[edit](https://en.wikiquote.org/w/index.php?title=Wikipedia&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2001")]

*   At present I am overworked and the [Nupedia] project is suffering to some extent as a result... I just don't have the time to find lead reviewers for the articles listed [in "General and Other"]. The problem is that it is VERY difficult to find *specialists* on each of those topics.
    *   [Larry Sanger](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Larry_Sanger "Larry Sanger"), [Thread: General and Other editor and editorial changes?](http://web.archive.org/web/20030503011149/http://www.nupedia.com/pipermail/nupedia-l/2001-January/000671.html), _Nupedia-l mailing list_ (5 January 2001)

*   It's an idea to add a little feature to Nupedia. ..."Wiki," pronounced \wee'-kee\, derives from a Polynesian word, "wikiwiki," but what it means is a VERY open, VERY publicly-editable series of web pages. ... I can start a page ... Anyone else (yes, absolutely anyone else) can come along and make absolutely any changes to it that he wants to. ... On the page I create, I can link to any other pages, and of course anyone can link to mine. The project is billed and pursued as a public resource. There are a few announced suggestions or rules. ... As to Nupedia's use of a wiki, this is the ULTIMATE "open" and simple format for developing content. We have occasionally bandied about ideas for simpler, more open projects to either replace or supplement Nupedia. ... [It] can be a place where additional changes and commentary can be gleaned... The content can be licensed under an open content license. On the front page of the Nupedia wiki we'd make it ABSOLUTELY clear that this is experimental... 
    *   [Larry Sanger](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Larry_Sanger "Larry Sanger"), [Thread: Let's make a wiki](http://web.archive.org/web/20030414014355/http://www.nupedia.com/pipermail/nupedia-l/2001-January/000676.html), _Nupedia-l mailing list_ (10 January 2001)

*   We wouldn't call it "the Nupedia wiki" though that's what it would be. ... On the "wikipedia" we would say that this is a supplementary project to Nupedia which operates entirely independently. 
    *   [Larry Sanger](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Larry_Sanger "Larry Sanger"), [Thread: Re: [Advisory-l](http://web.archive.org/web/20030414021138/http:/www.nupedia.com/pipermail/nupedia-l/2001-January/000680.html) The wiki...], _Nupedia-l mailing list_ (11 January 2001)

*   It was a cold Friday evening in January 2001. I was on duty in one of my uni's computer labs...

At first I was a bit intimidated about the entries and discussions, which I saw there. The main contributors at the time were Jimbo, Larry and w:Josh Grosse. The 'Pedia had ca. 700 (!) entries, and was still using the weird Camel Case format, which made links appear in the manner of w:PortugaL or w:PolanD. After a bit of lurking around I quickly figured out what the purpose of the project was, and came to the simple conclusion "Me likes thees!".What followed were normal symptoms of my gradual turning into a w:Wikipediholic. I spent a large portion of my free time starting entries, editing, and cross-linking. I witnessed the project grow gradually and in waves as it became more popular (slashdotting, etc.). During the Summer, doing the hard job of an analyst at a medium-sized Polish financial institution kept me away for a while. I was back in mid-September. And I intend to stay for as long as I can, or until my cable modem dies on me.
*       *   +wojpob

**Attingal** is a municipality and a northern suburb of the [Thiruvananthapuram Metropolitan Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_metropolitan_area "Thiruvananthapuram metropolitan area"), [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal#cite_note-3) It is the maternal home and ancestral residence of the Travancore Royal Family (Venad), and was ruled by the female royals ([Attingal Ranis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayamma_Rani "Umayamma Rani")) as Attingal Thirumoopil Swaroopam under [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore").

It is the headquarters of [Chirayinkeezhu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu "Chirayinkeezhu")[Taluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehsil "Tehsil"), and the important government institutions of the taluk such as the [Taluk office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taluka_office "Taluka office"), Court Complex, Office of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, Civil Station, and treasuries are situated in Attingal. It is one of the oldest municipalities of Kerala which was constituted prior to its independence in 1924. In 1914, Attingal Town Improvement Authority (TIA) was formed which was the term used before the Travancore Municipality Regulation Act of 1922 formed the Attingal Municipality. Attingal Town is located 30 kilometres (19 mi) north of [Thampanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram "Thiruvananthapuram"), the city centre. Attingal is the 3rd most densely populated municipality in the district.

**Kilimanoor Assembly constituency** was a constituency of the [Kerala Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_Legislative_Assembly "Kerala Legislative Assembly"). It consisted of [Pazhayakunnummel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazhayakunnummel "Pazhayakunnummel")[Pulimath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulimath "Pulimath"), [Kilimanoor Grama Panchayath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Grama_Panchayath "Kilimanoor Grama Panchayath"), [Nagaroor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagaroor "Nagaroor"), [Madavoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madavoor-Pallickal "Madavoor-Pallickal"), [Pallickal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pallickal,_Thiruvananthapuram "Pallickal, Thiruvananthapuram"), [Karavaram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karavaram "Karavaram"), [Mudakkal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudakkal "Mudakkal") and [Navaikulam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navaikulam "Navaikulam") Panchayats.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Assembly_Constituency#cite_note-2) Adv. N. Rajan was the last representative of this constituency from 2001 to 2006.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Assembly_Constituency#cite_note-3)

**Kilimanoor Palace** is a palace located in [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor "Kilimanoor"), in the Indian state of [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Palace#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Palace#cite_note-2) It is the birthplace of painter [Raja Ravi Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma "Raja Ravi Varma") and Raghava Varma, the father of king [Marthanda Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marthanda_Varma "Marthanda Varma").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Palace#cite_note-Thrippadidaanam-3)

## The Palace

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor_Palace&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: The Palace")]

The Palace complex covers more than six hectares, and comprises the traditional residential structures of Kerala, like the Nalukettu, small and medium-sized buildings, three ponds, wells and sacred groves (_kaavu_).

Raja Ravi Varma is said to have built and maintained some of the buildings from the proceeds of his paintings. Families related to the Travancore royal house continue to live here.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor_Palace&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

The royal house at Choottayil, [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor "Kilimanoor") has a history stretching back more than 300 years, although the oldest buildings are from a much earlier period.

### Association with the Travancore royal house

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor_Palace&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Association with the Travancore royal house")]

In 1705, the son and two daughters of Ittammar Raja of [Beypore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beypore "Beypore") Thattarikovilakam, the northern branch of [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad") royal house, were adopted into the royal house of [Venad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venad "Venad"). The Ittammar Raja's sister and her sons, Rama Varma and Raghava Varma, settled in Kilimanoor and married the now-adopted sisters.

The lands around the present-day palace were a part of an estate which originally belonged to a [Pillai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillai_(Kerala_title) "Pillai (Kerala title)") ruling chief. The estate comprised several villages and was handed over to the family of Raghava Varma.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Palace#cite_note-4)[Maharaja Marthanda Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marthanda_Varma "Marthanda Varma"), the founder of the [Kingdom of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"), was the son of Raghava Varma.

In 1739, after Marthanda Varma ascended the throne, an alliance led by the [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Malabar "Dutch Malabar") Captain Hockert, was formed between [Kochi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Malabar "Dutch Malabar"), [Thekkumkoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thekkumkur "Thekkumkur"), [Desinganadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kollam "Kollam") and [Purakkad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purakkad "Purakkad"), due to their shared enmity towards Marthanda Varma. In 1740, this [allied force attacked Venad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore%E2%80%93Dutch_War#Initial_Dutch_successes "Travancore–Dutch War") and an army from Kilimanoor resisted and subsequently defeated them in the [Battle of Colachel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Colachel "Battle of Colachel"). Although a small victory, this was the first time an Indian army had defeated a European power.

In 1753, in recognition of this feat, Marthanda Varma exempted the areas controlled by the Kilimanoor Palace, as well as most of the area under the present Kilimanoor and [Pazhayakunnummel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazhayakunnummel "Pazhayakunnummel") panchayats from taxes, and granted them autonomous status. Although the estate had been under his rule earlier, the present palace complex was built in 1753, together with the Ayyappa temple. The original temple was at Nerumkaithakotta, near Kozhikode for the family deity, Sastha or Ayyapan.

In the early 19th century, [Velu Thampi Dalawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velu_Thampi_Dalawa "Velu Thampi Dalawa") held meetings at Kilimanoor Palace while planning uprisings against the British. In 1809, he handed over his sword at the Palace before going into his final battle against the British. India's first President, [Dr Rajendra Prasad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajendra_Prasad "Rajendra Prasad") received this sword from the palace and it was kept in the [National Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum,_New_Delhi "National Museum, New Delhi") in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi"). Afterwards the sword was moved to the [Napier Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napier_Museum "Napier Museum") in Thiruvananthapuram.

**Kilimanoor** is a panchayat and a town in the [Chirayinkeezhu taluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu_taluk "Chirayinkeezhu taluk") of [Thiruvananthapuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district "Thiruvananthapuram district") in [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"), India.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor#cite_note-2) It is located on [MC/SH 1 Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_central_Road "Main central Road"), 33 kilometres (21 mi) northwest of the city of Thiruvananthapuram ([Trivandrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trivandrum "Trivandrum")), 14 km (8.7 mi) east of [Attingal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal") and 20 km (12 mi) east of [Varkala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varkala "Varkala").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Kilimanoor ("land of the bird and the deer") was ruled by a [Pillai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sai_pillai_meleputhiyakav_(Kerala_title)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sai pillai meleputhiyakav (Kerala title) (page does not exist)") ruling chief and was forfeited to Travancore by Maharaja Marthanda Varma. The estate comprising several villages was then handed over to the family of the father of the King who had come south from Parappanad in Malabar around 1718.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor#cite_note-3) was ruled by a chief during time of the [Ettuveetil Pillamar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ettuveetil_Pillamar "Ettuveetil Pillamar") in the kingdom of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"). The chief rebelled against the [Maharajah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharajah "Maharajah")[Marthanda Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marthanda_Varma "Marthanda Varma"), and the region was annexed and later given to the Royal House of Kilimanoor.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAiya1906329-4)

This [Royal House of Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_House_of_Kilimanoor "Royal House of Kilimanoor") has a history of more than 300 years. In 1705 (ME 880), the son and two daughters of Ittammar Raja of Beypore Thattarikovilakam, a [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad") royal house, were adopted by the Royal house of [Venad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venad "Venad"). Parappanad was actually the ruling family of [Parappanangadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanangadi "Parappanangadi") in present-day [Malappuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malappuram_district "Malappuram district"). Ittammar Raja's sister and her sons, Rama Varma and Raghava Varma, settled in Kilimanoor and married the now-adopted sisters. Marthanda Varma, the founder of the [Kingdom of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Travancore "Kingdom of Travancore") was the son of Raghava Varma. Raghava Varma's nephew, Ravi Varma Koil Thampuran, married Marthanda Varma's sister. Their son came to be known as Dharma Raja Kartika Thirunnal Rama Varma. In 1740, when an allied force led by Dutch Captain Hockert supporting the Deshinganadu king attacked Venad, an army from Kilimanoor tactfully resisted and then defeated them. Although a small victory, this was the first time an Indian army defeated a European power. In recognition of this feat, Marthanda Varma, in 1753, exempted the areas under control of [Kilimanoor Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Palace "Kilimanoor Palace") from taxes and proclaimed autonomous status. The present palace complex was also built during this time along with the Ayyappa temple for the family deity.

Velu Thampi Dalawa held meetings at the Kilimanoor Palace, planning his revolts against the [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj"). He handed over his sword at the palace before going for his final battle against the British. India's First President, [Dr. Rajendra Prasad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Rajendra_Prasad "Dr. Rajendra Prasad") received the sword from the palace, and it is now kept at the [National Museum, New Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum,_New_Delhi "National Museum, New Delhi"). Subsequently, placed at the Napier Museum in the capital city of Kerala.

## Transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Transportation")]

Kilimanoor is on the [Main Central Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Central_Road "Main Central Road"). It is connected to the whole major destination by buses run by [KSRTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_State_Road_Transport_Corporation "Kerala State Road Transport Corporation") from the Kilimanoor bus depot. Kilimanoor is only 33 kilometres (21 mi) away from [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram "Thiruvananthapuram"). The nearest airport is [Trivandrum International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trivandrum_International_Airport "Trivandrum International Airport"). The nearest major railway station is [Varkala Railway Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varkala_Railway_Station "Varkala Railway Station") which is 20 km (12 mi) from Kilimanoor.

**Attingal** is a municipality and a northern suburb of the [Thiruvananthapuram Metropolitan Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_metropolitan_area "Thiruvananthapuram metropolitan area"), [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal#cite_note-3) It is the maternal home and ancestral residence of the Travancore Royal Family (Venad), and was ruled by the female royals ([Attingal Ranis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayamma_Rani "Umayamma Rani")) as Attingal Thirumoopil Swaroopam under [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore").

It is the headquarters of [Chirayinkeezhu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu "Chirayinkeezhu")[Taluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehsil "Tehsil"), and the important government institutions of the taluk such as the [Taluk office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taluka_office "Taluka office"), Court Complex, Office of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, Civil Station, and treasuries are situated in Attingal. It is one of the oldest municipalities of Kerala which was constituted prior to its independence in 1924. In 1914, Attingal Town Improvement Authority (TIA) was formed which was the term used before the Travancore Municipality Regulation Act of 1922 formed the Attingal Municipality. Attingal Town is located 30 kilometres (19 mi) north of [Thampanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram "Thiruvananthapuram"), the city centre. Attingal is the 3rd most densely populated municipality in the district.

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Attingal&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

Attingal is widely believed to have derived its name from “Attinkara,” meaning “river banks,” referring to the Vamanapuram River that flows along the northern and southern boundaries of the municipality at Mamom and Poovanpara.

## Demographics and History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Attingal&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Demographics and History")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Attingal.jpg/250px-Attingal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Attingal.jpg)

[NH 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NH_66 "NH 66") at Attingal

According to the 2011 [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal#cite_note-4) Attingal has a population of 37,346. Males constitute 17,009 of the population and females 20,337.

According to 2011 Census data projected to 2026, the Attingal Municipality boasts a high average literacy rate of 96.65%, which is significantly higher than the Kerala state average of 94%. Male literacy in the town is approximately 97.71%, while female literacy is recorded at 95.77%.  The town is famed for its cleanliness in recent years. The municipality has undertaken many plans which have been successful. The municipality has also achieved a couple of awards for its success.

**History**

Attingal and anchuthengu Kalapam are the historical first riot against British government in Kerala.

Anchuthengu Kalapam/riot is at 1697 for selling the pepper issues made by British government it was the first riot in Kerala against British. Then [Attingal Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal_Outbreak "Attingal Outbreak") are done in 1721 were the first organised riot against British government, it settled by Venadu agreement.

## Tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Attingal&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Tourism")]

### Attingal Palace

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Attingal&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Attingal Palace")]

[Koyikkal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koyikkal_Palace "Koyikkal Palace") is the maternal home of the [Travancore royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore_royal_family "Travancore royal family"). The great rulers of the kingdom, including [Anizham Thirunal Marthanda Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anizham_Thirunal_Marthanda_Varma "Anizham Thirunal Marthanda Varma"), were brought up in this palace situated at Kollampuzha, Attingal.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal#cite_note-7) The palace, built in stone and wood, according to Kerala architecture stands in a nearly 10-acre wide plot, a portion of which is privately owned now. The palace has four temples inside it, including the 700-year-old sanctorum that houses the Palliyara Bhagavathy. The temple of the family deity, Thiruvarattukavu Devi, is also seated in a temple inside the palace complex.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal#cite_note-8) The historically important palace, built in an 'ettukettu' structure. The temples and the palace is currently under the control of the Devaswom Board. One of the entrance gates here, ' Chavadipura', was reconstructed recently by the royal family.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal#cite_note-9)

### Anchuthengu Fort

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Attingal&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Anchuthengu Fort")]

The historical fort of [Anchuthengu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Thiruvananthapuram#Anchuthengu "Tourism in Thiruvananthapuram") is about 10 km from Attingal town and the famous [Siva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiva "Shiva") temple [Avanavanchery Sri Indilayappan Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avanavanchery_Sri_Indilayappan_Temple "Avanavanchery Sri Indilayappan Temple") and Veerakeralapuram Sreekrishna Swami Temple are within the Attingal Municipal area.

**Kumaran ashan Smarakam**

The historical museum of Kerala renaissance leader and poet [Kumaran Asan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumaran_Asan "Kumaran Asan") situated in Thonnakkal, Attingal have Kumaran ashan home made with grass and his works and belongings are showed in museum.[](https://www.keralatourism.org/kerala-article/2024/asan-smarakam-thonnakkal-thiruvananthapuram-poet-literary-legend/1408)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Attingal&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Transport")]

Attingal is one of the important hubs of the Thiruvananthapuram district. [Kanyakumari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanyakumari "Kanyakumari")-[Panvel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panvel "Panvel") Highway([National Highway 66 (India)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Highway_66_(India) "National Highway 66 (India)")) along with [SH 46](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Highway_46_(Kerala) "State Highway 46 (Kerala)") and [SH 47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Highway_47_(Kerala) "State Highway 47 (Kerala)") connecting the town to [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor "Kilimanoor") and [Nedumangadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nedumangadu "Nedumangadu"), passes through the town.SH46 joins the Town at [Alamcode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alamcode,_Thiruvananthapuram "Alamcode, Thiruvananthapuram") and SH47 at Munumukku. Both KSRTC and private buses have frequent services to nearby towns like [Varkala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varkala "Varkala"), [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor "Kilimanoor"), [Kallambalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kallambalam "Kallambalam"), [Chirayinkeezhu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu "Chirayinkeezhu"), [Kadakkavoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kadakkavoor "Kadakkavoor"), [Venjarammoodu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venjarammoodu "Venjarammoodu"), [Nedumangad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nedumangad "Nedumangad"), [Karette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karette?action=edit&redlink=1 "Karette (page does not exist)"), [Vamanapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vamanapuram "Vamanapuram"), [Madathara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madathara "Madathara"), including back-to-back Electric Buses and City Shuttle buses between [Technopark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technopark,_Trivandrum "Technopark, Trivandrum"), [Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_International_Airport "Thiruvananthapuram International Airport"), [Medical College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Medical_College,_Thiruvananthapuram "Government Medical College, Thiruvananthapuram") and [East Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Fort "East Fort"). There are also long distance buses to nearly all major cities in Kerala including [Kollam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kollam "Kollam"), [Ernakulam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernakulam "Ernakulam"), [Kozhikode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kozhikode "Kozhikode"), [Thrissur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrissur "Thrissur"), [Malappuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malappuram "Malappuram"), etc. The nearest railway stations are [Chirayinkeezhu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu "Chirayinkeezhu") Railway station (7 km), [Kadakkavoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kadakkavoor "Kadakkavoor") Railway station (8 km), and [Kazhakkottam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazhakuttam_railway_station "Kazhakuttam railway station") Railway Station (15km), with the closest major railway station being [Varkala Sivagiri Railway Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varkala_Sivagiri_railway_station "Varkala Sivagiri railway station") (15 km). [Thiruvananthapuram International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_International_Airport "Thiruvananthapuram International Airport") (33 km) is the nearest airport. Two dedicated bus depots are available in the forms of a [Kerala State Road Transport Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_State_Road_Transport_Corporation "Kerala State Road Transport Corporation")(KSRTC) bus depot which is one among the 28 Main depots of KSRTC and one Private Bus Terminal, both in the heart of the town. A bypass as part of NH66 6-laning is being constructed that diverts from Mamom and ends at Ayamkonam, that completely avoids the Attingal Municipality limits to reduce traffic bottlenecks. Attingal has been a large traffic bottleneck in Thiruvananthapuram especially on NH66.

**Kilimanoor Palace** is a palace located in [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor "Kilimanoor"), in the Indian state of [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_House_of_Kilimanoor#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_House_of_Kilimanoor#cite_note-2) It is the birthplace of painter [Raja Ravi Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma "Raja Ravi Varma") and Raghava Varma, the father of king [Marthanda Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marthanda_Varma "Marthanda Varma").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_House_of_Kilimanoor#cite_note-Thrippadidaanam-3)

## The Palace

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor_Palace&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: The Palace")]

The Palace complex covers more than six hectares, and comprises the traditional residential structures of Kerala, like the Nalukettu, small and medium-sized buildings, three ponds, wells and sacred groves (_kaavu_).

Raja Ravi Varma is said to have built and maintained some of the buildings from the proceeds of his paintings. Families related to the Travancore royal house continue to live here.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor_Palace&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

The royal house at Choottayil, [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor "Kilimanoor") has a history stretching back more than 300 years, although the oldest buildings are from a much earlier period.

### Association with the Travancore royal house

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kilimanoor_Palace&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Association with the Travancore royal house")]

In 1705, the son and two daughters of Ittammar Raja of [Beypore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beypore "Beypore") Thattarikovilakam, the northern branch of [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad") royal house, were adopted into the royal house of [Venad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venad "Venad"). The Ittammar Raja's sister and her sons, Rama Varma and Raghava Varma, settled in Kilimanoor and married the now-adopted sisters.

The lands around the present-day palace were a part of an estate which originally belonged to a [Pillai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillai_(Kerala_title) "Pillai (Kerala title)") ruling chief. The estate comprised several villages and was handed over to the family of Raghava Varma.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_House_of_Kilimanoor#cite_note-4)[Maharaja Marthanda Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marthanda_Varma "Marthanda Varma"), the founder of the [Kingdom of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"), was the son of Raghava Varma.

In 1739, after Marthanda Varma ascended the throne, an alliance led by the [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Malabar "Dutch Malabar") Captain Hockert, was formed between [Kochi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Malabar "Dutch Malabar"), [Thekkumkoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thekkumkur "Thekkumkur"), [Desinganadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kollam "Kollam") and [Purakkad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purakkad "Purakkad"), due to their shared enmity towards Marthanda Varma. In 1740, this [allied force attacked Venad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore%E2%80%93Dutch_War#Initial_Dutch_successes "Travancore–Dutch War") and an army from Kilimanoor resisted and subsequently defeated them in the [Battle of Colachel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Colachel "Battle of Colachel"). Although a small victory, this was the first time an Indian army had defeated a European power.

In 1753, in recognition of this feat, Marthanda Varma exempted the areas controlled by the Kilimanoor Palace, as well as most of the area under the present Kilimanoor and [Pazhayakunnummel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazhayakunnummel "Pazhayakunnummel") panchayats from taxes, and granted them autonomous status. Although the estate had been under his rule earlier, the present palace complex was built in 1753, together with the Ayyappa temple. The original temple was at Nerumkaithakotta, near Kozhikode for the family deity, Sastha or Ayyapan.

In the early 19th century, [Velu Thampi Dalawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velu_Thampi_Dalawa "Velu Thampi Dalawa") held meetings at Kilimanoor Palace while planning uprisings against the British. In 1809, he handed over his sword at the Palace before going into his final battle against the British. India's first President, [Dr Rajendra Prasad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajendra_Prasad "Rajendra Prasad") received this sword from the palace and it was kept in the [National Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum,_New_Delhi "National Museum, New Delhi") in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi"). Afterwards the sword was moved to the [Napier Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napier_Museum "Napier Museum") in Thiruvananthapuram.

##### A reknowned palace in Kerala, renowned as the birthplace of Raja Ravi Varma, showcasing traditional Kerala architecture, a preserved art studio, and a legacy of cultural and artistic significance.

Kilimanoor Palace, located in the Kilimanoor village of Thiruvananthapuram district, Kerala, is a historic and culturally significant landmark. This sprawling complex, with its traditional Kerala architecture, lush surroundings, and rich history, offers visitors a fascinating glimpse into the royal heritage of Kerala. The palace is particularly renowned as the birthplace of the celebrated Indian painter Raja Ravi Varma, making it an essential destination for art lovers, history enthusiasts, and tourists.  
  
**Historical Significance**  
Kilimanoor Palace has a history that spans several centuries, dating back to the early 18th century. The palace was originally built by the royal family of Travancore as a residential and administrative center. Over the years, it has been the site of significant historical events and has hosted many distinguished guests, including British officials and Indian royalty. The most notable historical figure associated with Kilimanoor Palace is Raja Ravi Varma, one of India's greatest painters. Born in 1848, Ravi Varma is celebrated for his pioneering work in Indian art, blending traditional Indian themes with European techniques. The palace remains a symbol of his artistic legacy and continues to attract art aficionados from around the world.  
  
**Architectural Features**  
Kilimanoor Palace is an exemplar of traditional Kerala architecture, featuring wide verandahs, spacious courtyards, and long corridors. The palace's red-tiled roofs and brilliant white walls add to its picturesque charm. The architectural design incorporates local materials like wood and laterite stone, reflecting the indigenous construction techniques of the time.  
  
**Raja Ravi Varma Studio**  
The Chitrashala studio, designed by Raja Ravi Varma and built around 1875, is a significant part of Kilimanoor Palace. The studio boasts large glass windows that flood the space with natural light, creating an ideal environment for painting. It houses a dusty, aged easel and other tools used by Varma. The serene and inspiring surroundings include views of the flowering garden and paddy fields, which influenced Varma's works.  
  
**Cultural and Artistic Significance**  
Kilimanoor Palace is not only a historical site but also a cultural hub that celebrates the artistic heritage of Kerala. The palace's association with Raja Ravi Varma adds immense cultural value, as his works played a crucial role in shaping modern Indian art. Varma's paintings are renowned for their depictions of Hindu mythology, portraits of Indian women, and use of vibrant colors and intricate details. The palace preserves his memory with prints of his famous paintings, photographs, and personal artifacts. The Kilimanoor Palace Trust continues to uphold Varma's legacy by maintaining the palace and organizing events to celebrate his contributions to art. The palace regularly hosts art exhibitions, cultural programs, and workshops, promoting the arts and preserving the legacy of Raja Ravi Varma. Visitors can explore the museum dedicated to his works, attend lectures on his contributions to art, and participate in activities that highlight the rich cultural heritage of Kerala.  
  
**Accommodation**  
There are several accommodation options available in and around Kilimanoor, ranging from budget lodgings to luxury resorts. Many of these establishments offer comfortable stays with modern amenities, providing a convenient base for exploring Kilimanoor Palace and the surrounding attractions.  
  
**Visitor Information**  
The best time to visit Kilimanoor Palace is year-round, as its indoor setting ensures that weather conditions do not impact the experience, making it ideal for sightseeing and exploring the palace at any time.  
  
Hiring a local guide can enhance the visitor experience by providing detailed information about the historical and cultural significance of the palace. Guides can also offer insights into the life and works of Raja Ravi Varma and the architectural features of the complex.  
  
Kilimanoor Palace, with its historical significance, architectural splendor, and cultural heritage, offers a unique and enriching experience for visitors. Whether you are an art enthusiast, a history buff, or a curious traveler, the palace provides a fascinating glimpse into the royal legacy and artistic traditions of Kerala. A visit to Kilimanoor Palace is not only an educational journey but also an opportunity to connect with the timeless beauty and cultural richness of Kerala's past.

**Chirayinkeezhu Taluk** is a [taluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taluk "Taluk") in the district of [Thiruvananthapuram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district "Thiruvananthapuram district") in the Indian state of [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu_taluk#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu_taluk#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu_taluk#cite_note-3) It shares a land border with [Varkala Taluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varkala_Taluk "Varkala Taluk") to the North and [Thiruvananthapuram Taluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_Taluk "Thiruvananthapuram Taluk") to the South. It comprises 12 panchayats as well as [Attingal Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal"). Chirayinkeezhu taluk is the birthplace of several distinguished personalities, including the renowned painter [Raja Ravi Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma "Raja Ravi Varma"), poet and social reformer [Kumaran Asan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumaran_Asan "Kumaran Asan"), and the actor [Prem Nazir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prem_Nazir "Prem Nazir").

The estate of Kilimanoor originally belonged to a [Pillai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillai_(Kerala_title) "Pillai (Kerala title)") ruling chief and was forfeited to Travancore by Maharaja Marthanda Varma. The estate comprising several villages was then handed over to the family of the father of the King who had come south from Parappanad in Malabar around 1718.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirayinkeezhu_taluk#cite_note-6)

In 1705 ([ME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam_era "Malayalam era") 880) the son and two daughters of Ittammar Raja of [Beypore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beypore "Beypore") Thattarikovilakam, a [Kolathunadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolathunadu "Kolathunadu") royal house, were adopted into the Royal house of [Venad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venad "Venad"). Ittammar Raja's sister and her sons, Rama Varma and Raghava Varma, settled in Kilimanoor and married the now adopted sisters. [Marthanda Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marthanda_Varma "Marthanda Varma"), the founder of the Kingdom of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"), was the son of Raghava Varma. The nephew Sister's son. According to the matrilineal system prevalent at that time children born of the female members only belonged to that house of Raghava Varma, Ravi varma Koil Thampuran, married the sister of Marthanda Varma. Their son became known as [Dharma Raja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharma_Raja "Dharma Raja") Kartika Thirunnal Rama Varma.

In 1740 when an allied force, the forces were from Kochi, Thekkumkoor, Deshinganad (present kollam) and Purakkad who had enmity towards Marthanda Varma led by Dutchman Captain Hockert supporting the Deshinganadu King, attacked Venad, an army from Kilimanoor resisted and then defeated them. Although a small victory, this was the first time an Indian army had defeated a European power. In 1753, in recognition of this feat, Marthanda Varma exempted the areas controlled by the Kilimanoor palace. Most of the area under the present Kilimanoor and _Pazhayakunnummel_[panchayats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panchayati_raj "Panchayati raj"). from taxes, and granted them autonomous status. Although under his kingdom. The present palace complex was built at this time, together with the Ayyappa temple. The original temple being at _Nerumkaithakotta_, near Kozhikode for the family deity, _Sastha_ or Ayyapan.

[Velu Thampi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velu_Thampi_Dalawa "Velu Thampi Dalawa")[Dalawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewan "Dewan") held meetings at Kilimanoor palace while planning uprisings against the British. He handed over his sword at the palace before going into his final battle against the British, and India's first President, Dr [Rajendra Prasad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajendra_Prasad "Rajendra Prasad") received this sword from the palace and it was kept in the [National Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum,_New_Delhi "National Museum, New Delhi") in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi"). Afterwards the sword was moved to the Napier Museum, Trivandrum.
